clinicalPearls: Most common cause of dementia, contributing an estimated 60-70% of all cases; in the U.S. ~10% of people over 65 have AD (3% at age 65-74, 17% at 75-84, 32% at 85+) (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478).

Typical presentation is insidious loss of episodic memory followed by slowly progressive multidomain dementia, with cognitive change progressing from memory to executive, language, and visuospatial deficits (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476).

About 20% of patients present with nonmemory complaints; atypical variants include posterior cortical atrophy (visual processing), logopenic progressive aphasia, corticobasal (akinetic-rigid-dystonic) syndrome, and a dysexecutive/behavioral (frontal) variant (Harrison 22e p.3475-3476).
Depression, social withdrawal, and anxiety may occur early and represent a prodrome before cognitive symptoms are apparent (Harrison 22e p.3476).

~50% of patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), roughly 12% per year, progress to dementia over 4 years; the MCI construct is increasingly replaced by 'early symptomatic AD' (Harrison 22e p.3476).
Preclinical biomarker changes may precede clinical symptoms by 20 years or more, creating a window for early treatment and prevention (Harrison 22e p.3476).

Core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) are considered necessary and sufficient for biological diagnosis of AD under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria; tau PET is a core 2 biomarker used for staging (Harrison 22e p.3477).
A negative amyloid PET scan in a patient with dementia makes an AD diagnosis unlikely; a positive scan can establish eligibility for amyloid-lowering therapy (Harrison 22e p.3477).

Decreases in the CSF Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio and increases in p-Tau181 or p-Tau217 correlate with AD pathology; plasma biomarkers show high concordance with amyloid PET and are entering clinical use (Harrison 22e p.3477).

ApoE epsilon4 is the most important genetic risk factor for sporadic AD: one allele raises risk ~2-3 fold (higher in women), two alleles raise it ~10-15 fold; each allele shifts onset ~10 years earlier (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3479-3480).

Lecanemab (anti-Abeta protofibril) and donanemab (anti-pyroglutamate Abeta) are FDA-approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies for early-stage AD, showing ~22-27% slowing of clinical decline; restricted to MCI/mild dementia with biomarker-confirmed Abeta pathology (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481).

Antiamyloid antibodies carry risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema, ARIA-H microhemorrhage/siderosis); risk rises with each ApoE epsilon4 allele and is highest in epsilon4 homozygotes, prompting an FDA box warning (Harrison 22e p.3481).

Treatment with lecanemab or donanemab should be considered a contraindication to peripheral thrombolysis, as catastrophic multifocal hemorrhages and death have been reported when antiamyloid-treated patients received thrombolytics for stroke (Harrison 22e p.3482).
Medications with strong anticholinergic effects (e.g., diphenhydramine sleep aids, oxybutynin) should be vigilantly avoided in AD (Harrison 22e p.3482).

Typical symptomatic duration is 8-10 years (range 1-25 years); death often results from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, heart disease, or, most commonly, aspiration (Harrison 22e p.3476).
harrison.pathophysiology: AD is characterized by extracellular neuritic plaques containing amyloid beta (Abeta) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) of hyperphosphorylated tau, with Abeta also accumulating in cortical and leptomeningeal blood vessel walls (amyloid angiopathy). Abeta is a 39-42 amino acid peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by beta and gamma secretases; excess production of Abeta42 is a key initiator of cellular damage, and soluble oligomers are thought to be the early toxic species before fibril/plaque formation. Hyperphosphorylated tau can no longer stabilize microtubules and redistributes from axon to cytoplasm and dendrites, with prion-like templating proposed to drive tau spread. Earliest and most severe degeneration is in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal/perirhinal cortex, hippocampus), inferolateral temporal cortex, and nucleus basalis of Meynert; atrophy spreads to temporoparietal and frontal cortices. Biochemically there is depletion of acetylcholine (degeneration of cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert neurons) plus noradrenergic and serotonergic loss from locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe. Genetic contributors include autosomal dominant mutations in APP (chromosome 21), PSEN-1 (chromosome 14, most common cause of early-onset familial AD), and PSEN-2 (chromosome 1), plus the ApoE epsilon4 risk allele (chromosome 19) and >40 minor GWAS risk variants in innate immunity, lipid metabolism, and synaptic pathways (e.g., CLU, PICALM, CR1, TREM2). (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478-3480)
additionalDifferentials: Vascular dementia (early prominent gait disturbance with only mild memory loss) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Dementia with Lewy bodies (early parkinsonism with fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, delusional misidentification) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Parkinson's disease / Parkinson's disease dementia (resting tremor, stooped posture, bradykinesia, masked facies) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Frontotemporal dementia (prominent behavioral changes with intact navigation and focal anterior-predominant atrophy) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease / prion disease (rapid progression over weeks-months with rigidity and myoclonus) (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482)

Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) and primary age-related tauopathy (PART) - can mimic AD clinically, especially in biomarker-negative older patients with progressive amnestic dementia (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3477)
Huntington's disease and rare hereditary ataxias when family history of dementia is present (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Primary or metastatic brain neoplasm (early focal seizure) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
infectionMimics: Viral or bacterial encephalitides (listed as causes of rapidly progressive dementia in the CJD differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483)
nonInfectiousMimics: Vitamin B12 deficiency (loss of joint position and vibration sensibility with Babinski signs; especially with autoimmune disease, small bowel resection/irradiation, or veganism) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Chronic drug intoxication (history of treatment for insomnia, anxiety, psychiatric disturbance, or epilepsy) (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Thyroid and other reversible/metabolic causes of dementia to be excluded per Tables 31-1, 31-3, 31-4 (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS lymphoma, paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (rapidly progressive dementia differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483)
additionalInvestigations: MRI/CT structural imaging - mainly to exclude other disorders; AD shows posterior-predominant cortical and medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy and may be normal early (Harrison 22e p.3476)
FDG-PET - shows hypometabolism in posterior temporal-parietal cortex (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Amyloid PET ([11C]PIB, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]florbetaben, [18F]flutemetamol) - confirms neuritic/diffuse Abeta plaques (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Tau PET ([18F]flortaucipir and research tracers) - estimates density/distribution of neurofibrillary tangles (Harrison 22e p.3476-3477)
CSF biomarkers - decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217 (Harrison 22e p.3477)
Plasma biomarkers - decreased Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio, increased p-Tau181/p-Tau217/p-Tau231 (Harrison 22e p.3477)
EEG - usually normal or nonspecific slowing; prolonged EEG to seek intermittent nonconvulsive seizures (Harrison 22e p.3476)
ApoE genotyping - recommended before initiating anti-Abeta antibody therapy to inform ARIA risk (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481)
Systemic laboratory tests to exclude reversible dementia mimics (Harrison 22e p.3476)
redFlags: Rapid progression over weeks to months with rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than AD (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482)
Early prominent gait disturbance with mild memory loss suggests vascular dementia or normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Early focal seizure suggests a metastatic or primary brain neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Loss of joint position/vibration sense with Babinski signs suggests vitamin B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3476)
Stroke-like symptoms in a patient on anti-Abeta monoclonal antibody require immediate MRI to differentiate acute stroke from ARIA before any thrombolysis (Harrison 22e p.3482)
Seizures (focal or generalized) can herald AD and occur even before dementia onset, especially in younger patients and autosomal dominant mutation carriers (Harrison 22e p.3476)
harrison.prognosis: Typical duration of symptomatic AD is 8-10 years, with a course ranging from 1 to 25 years. Some patients decline steadily while others have prolonged plateaus. Late stages bring rigidity, mutism, incontinence, and a bedridden state with dependence for eating, dressing, and toileting; hyperactive tendon reflexes and myoclonic jerks may occur. Death most commonly results from aspiration, and also from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, or heart disease. Approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies slow but do not halt clinical decline (~22-27% slowing over the trial periods). (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3480-3481)
pitfalls: Failing to exclude reversible/treatable mimics early in the course - vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and depression-related cognitive impairment should be excluded before attributing dementia to AD (Harrison 22e p.3476).

A clinical diagnosis of AD is confirmed at autopsy only ~70-80% of the time; misdiagnoses are usually LATE (with or without hippocampal sclerosis), PART, Lewy body disease, vascular pathology, or FTLD (Harrison 22e p.3476).

Amyloid PET positivity is not specific: ~25% of cognitively unimpaired older adults have positive scans, and a positive scan can reflect comorbid (incidental) AD pathology rather than the primary cause of impairment (Harrison 22e p.3476).
A completely negative tau PET does not rule out early neurofibrillary pathology (Braak stages I-III) (Harrison 22e p.3477).
Increased total tau in CSF is nonspecific - seen in AD but also other neurodegeneration (Harrison 22e p.3477).

Plasma Abeta and p-Tau concentrations can be altered by comorbidities (reduced creatinine clearance, elevated BMI), causing false-positive or false-negative results near the threshold (Harrison 22e p.3477).
ApoE epsilon4 is neither necessary nor sufficient to cause AD - many AD patients lack epsilon4 and many epsilon4 carriers never develop dementia (Harrison 22e p.3479-3480).

Estrogen, statins, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, and NSAIDs appeared protective in observational studies but did NOT show efficacy in randomized controlled trials; consumer 'memory-enhancing' supplements lack evidence (Harrison 22e p.3478, p.3482).
Antipsychotics carry an FDA black box warning in elderly dementia patients (increased risk of death) and should be used with caution for neuropsychiatric symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3482).
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical staging is performed independent of biomarkers, based on functional impairment along a continuum: preclinical AD (biomarker evidence of amyloid pathology without symptoms) -> subjective cognitive decline -> mild cognitive impairment / early symptomatic AD (functionally compensated) -> dementia stages (early/middle/late/end-stage). Biological staging under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria uses core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) for diagnosis and tau PET (core 2) for biomarker-based disease staging. (Harrison 22e p.3476-3478)
